To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the use of a single measurement of blood pressure to diagnose hypertension is associated with a high prevalence of misclassification, (b) the use of the average of two or more measurements improves the diagnosis, (c) the use of self-measured blood pressure improves the diagnosis of hypertension, and (d) self-measurement of blood pressure at home is associated with less misclassification than ambulatory blood pressure monitoring.

home blood pressure measurements are associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular disease, and that home measurements are better than office or clinic measurements at identifying people with high blood pressure who are at increased risk for cardiovascular disease.
the use of a self-measured blood pressure monitor (SMBPM) is a feasible and valid approach for the diagnosis of hypertension and the assessment of target organ damage in patients with hypertension.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the home measurement of blood pressure (BP), as a non invasive method, has been widely used in the diagnosis of arterial hypertension and in the assessment of target organ damage (TOD), but there are still doubts about the reliability of the home measurement of BP.

the use of home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) in patients with hypertension has been increasing in Spain in recent years, and that the use of ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) has also increased, but to a lesser extent.
home self-measurements (HSM) of blood pressure (BP) are useful in the diagnosis of hypertension and in identifying target organ damage.

the relationship between self-measurement of blood pressure and the diagnosis of hypertension and organ damage is similar to that observed with ambulatory monitoring of blood pressure.

the relationship between blood pressure and mortality risk is continuous, and that the relationship between systolic blood pressure and mortality is stronger than the relationship between diastolic blood pressure and risk of death.
home self-monitoring is not only feasible but can be used to identify patients who are at risk of developing cardiovascular disease.
